notes.meaning: Jethro, a priest and leader in Midian, heard about all the miracles God had done to rescue Israel from Egypt. He recognized that the Lord, not human skill, had set the people free. Hearing the news moved him to travel out to the desert to see Moses.

Earlier, Moses had sent his wife Zipporah back home to Midian, likely to keep her safe from the troubles and dangers in Egypt. Now that God had delivered the people, Jethro brought her back so the family could be together again. God cares about family life even in the middle of great events.

Moses had named his two sons to remember how God cared for him in the past. Gershom meant he had lived as a stranger in a foreign land, while Eliezer meant God was his helper who saved him from Pharaoh's sword. Remembering how God helped us yesterday gives us courage for today.

Jethro brought Moses' wife and sons to the camp near Mount Sinai, also called the mountain of God. This mountain was holy ground because the Lord had appeared to Moses there at the burning bush. God was now bringing Moses back to the very place where He first called him.

Jethro sent a message ahead to tell Moses that he was arriving with Moses' wife and sons. Sending word ahead gave Moses time to prepare a warm welcome. It showed Jethro's respect and courtesy toward the leader of Israel.

Moses went out to greet his father-in-law, bowing down and kissing him in the customary greeting of the ancient Near East. Even though Moses was now the leader of a huge nation, he remained humble and honored his elder. They asked about each other's well-being and went into the tent to talk.

Moses told Jethro the full story of how the Lord defeated Pharaoh and brought Israel out of slavery. He did not hide their hardships along the way, but explained how the Lord rescued them each time. Sharing stories of God's faithfulness strengthens the faith of those who listen.

Jethro rejoiced with deep joy over all the good things the Lord had done for Israel. As an outsider, he was moved by God's mercy and celebrated Israel's blessings with a sincere heart. True believers are always glad when they see God blessing others.

Jethro praised the Lord for saving Moses and the Israelites from the power of Egypt. He recognized that their escape was not just human luck, but the direct work of God's hand. Giving praise to God is the right response to every answered prayer and rescue.

Jethro declared that the Lord is greater than all other gods because He completely defeated the proud Egyptians. The Egyptian rulers had treated Israel cruelly, but the Lord proved He was far stronger than their idols. God humbles the proud and defends those who cannot defend themselves.

differ.view: Jethro was already a worshipper of the true God through the patriarchal faith of Abraham, and this event simply confirmed what he already believed.
Jethro had previously held a confused faith mixed with the errors of surrounding nations, and he was brought to a genuine and clear knowledge of the true God here.

notes.meaning: Jethro offered animal sacrifices to thank and honor the true God. Aaron and the elders of Israel joined him in a sacred meal, eating together in God's presence. Worshiping and eating together united them in peace and shared gratitude to the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest this account reflects an early tradition where Midianites introduced Moses and Israel to the worship of Yahweh.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Encyclopedia views this sacred meal as sealing a formal covenant or alliance between Israel and the Midianites.

notes.meaning: The next morning, Moses sat as judge to settle disputes and answer legal questions for the people. A vast crowd stood waiting around him from morning until evening to have their problems heard. Moses showed great dedication to his calling, but working entirely alone was overwhelming.

When Jethro saw this routine, he asked Moses why he sat alone as judge while all the people waited around him all day long. Jethro was not questioning Moses' authority, but his method of handling the workload. Good leaders benefit from outside observers who can see when a system is not working well.

Moses explained that the people came to him to seek God's will and resolve their arguments. His role was to decide disputes fairly and teach them God's rules and laws. Moses saw himself as God's servant passing on divine truth rather than making up his own rules.

Jethro warned Moses that trying to do everything by himself was not good. Working from dawn to dusk would exhaust Moses, and making the people wait endlessly would wear out their patience. Even the most gifted leaders cannot carry every responsibility alone.

Jethro offered wise counsel and prayed that God would be with Moses. He told Moses to continue acting as the people's mediator, bringing their major issues and prayers directly before God. A leader's highest task is to pray and intercede for the people.

Jethro told Moses to focus on teaching God's laws and instructions to the whole nation. By learning how to live and what duties God expected, the people would be able to solve many small problems on their own. Teaching God's truth equips the community to walk in righteousness.

Jethro advised Moses to choose capable, God-fearing men who loved the truth and hated bribes or dishonest gain. These trustworthy men would serve as leaders over groups of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. Godly character and honest hearts are essential qualities for any leader.

These newly appointed judges were to handle the smaller everyday disputes at all times. Only the most difficult cases would go up to Moses, which would lighten his workload and share the responsibility. Sharing the work allows justice to be served quickly and fairly.

Jethro added that Moses should only adopt this plan if God commanded it. If God approved the plan, Moses would have the strength to endure, and the people could return to their tents satisfied and at peace. Good human advice must always be tested against God's direction.

Moses humbly listened to his father-in-law's advice and put it into practice. Even though Moses was a great prophet, he was willing to learn from an older relative. Truly wise leaders remain teachable and open to good counsel.

Moses appointed capable men across the tribes of Israel to serve as leaders over groups of various sizes. They judged ordinary disputes day by day and brought only the hardest problems to Moses. This orderly system provided relief for Moses and prompt help for the nation.

After his visit was over, Moses sent Jethro off with honor, and Jethro returned to his home country of Midian. Jethro came to rejoice with Moses, offered sound advice, and then departed without seeking power for himself. God often uses friends and family to bring timely help when we need it most.
